state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's imagine you have a group of friends who are all different heights. If everyone in the group suddenly grew by the same amount, would the tallest and shortest person still be the same? Think about how this relates to changing the heights of the plants in our scenario.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if everyone grew by 3cm, the tallest person would still be the tallest and the shortest would still be the shortest, so the difference between them wouldn't change... so Katie would be right too? But I'm still confused about Tom's answer - if we cut all the plants in half, does the range change or not?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about a group of friends again, but this time imagine they are all lined up in order of height. If everyone in the group suddenly shrank by the same proportion, would the order change? How does this relate to cutting the plants in half?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses analogies that fail to address the mathematical distinction between additive and multiplicative changes on range, and critically, the analogy about 'shrinking by the same proportion' misleadingly suggests order preservation implies range preservation, which is mathematically incorrect for proportional changes.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete real-world analogies (friends of different heights growing or shrinking) to help the student understand the abstract mathematical concept of range, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
